challenges.challenge: Write a thank-you note to someone who helps your school, such as a custodian, a bus driver, or a lunch helper.
challenges.why: Kendall County 4-H members packed notes with snacks for crews at the grain elevators. A thank-you note tells someone their work matters, and it does not cost anything.
challenges.school: Students write the note in class. The teacher hands the stack to a custodian, bus driver, or lunch helper the class already knows.
challenges.home: Write a note to someone in your home who does a job the family counts on, and leave it where they will find it.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, leave a thank-you at a library desk your family already uses. Stay with that grown-up.
challenges.teacherNote: Five quiet minutes is enough for the note. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Deliver anything the class made yourself, and do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a thank-you note for someone who helps at your school. It is free, and a teacher can deliver the notes.

challenges.challenge: Draw a small picture, write one hopeful sentence, and give it to a classmate or someone in your family.
challenges.why: Friends of Woodston Library in Peterborough are making seed packets with hopeful notes to give away. A drawing and one kind sentence can carry that same idea.
challenges.school: Students draw in class and trade cards with a partner they already sit near.
challenges.home: Leave the drawing on a family member's pillow or beside their plate.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, tuck the drawing into a library book you are returning. Stay together, and do not hand it to someone you do not know.
challenges.teacherNote: Colored pencils and scrap paper are enough. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Deliver anything the class made yourself, and do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a hopeful drawing and one kind sentence for someone you already know.

challenges.challenge: Make a small thank-you, such as a paper card, and give it to a grown-up your family already knows.
challenges.why: Kids in Bluefield dressed up and brought candy to shops as a thank-you, instead of only collecting it. A paper card for someone you already know is a safe way to try the same idea.
challenges.school: The class writes thank-you cards for the school office, and the teacher delivers them.
challenges.home: Make a paper card at the kitchen table and give it to a grown-up in your home.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, thank a neighbor your family already knows. Do not go to a door you do not know.
challenges.teacherNote: Keep the thank-you inside the group of people the students already know. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a small thank-you for a grown-up your family already knows. Nothing to buy, and no one new to meet.

challenges.challenge: Choose a finished book that is still in good shape, then pass it to a classmate, a sibling, or your school library.
challenges.why: Three bookshops in Saint-Brieuc are collecting extra children's books so more kids have something new to read. Sharing a finished book you already own is a free way to join in.
challenges.school: Set out a classroom basket for finished books students are ready to share, and add those books to the school library if the librarian says yes.
challenges.home: Read one page of a shared book aloud with someone you live with.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, leave a finished book in a Little Free Library your family already uses. Stay together.
challenges.teacherNote: Check that shared books are appropriate and still in one piece. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is sharing a finished book with someone you know or with your school library.

challenges.challenge: Make a paper bookmark and give it to a classmate who likes to read.
challenges.why: A 10-year-old in Valdosta made bracelets by hand and turned them into food, water, and supplies for people who needed them. A paper bookmark is a free way to make something for someone else.
challenges.school: Cut paper bookmarks in class and let each student write a classmate's name on one.
challenges.home: Make a bookmark for someone in your home and slip it into a book they are reading.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, leave the bookmark in a library book you are returning. Stay together.
challenges.teacherNote: Scrap paper and markers are enough. No one needs to bring money. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a handmade paper bookmark for a reader you already know.

challenges.challenge: Help pack a snack, or write a lunch note, for someone in your own home.
challenges.why: A volunteer in Aurora keeps packing weekend food bags for kids. Helping with one snack, or slipping a note into a lunch, is a small version of that care.
challenges.school: Students write a short lunch note and take their own note home to pack with a snack a grown-up approves. Do not require families to buy anything.
challenges.home: Help a grown-up pack a lunch, and add a one-sentence note.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, add one shelf-stable item you already have at home to a food drive your school or library is already running. Do not ask strangers for food.
challenges.teacherNote: Do not require a family to buy food for this challenge. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a snack or a lunch note for someone in your own home.

challenges.challenge: Invite a classmate into a game you are already playing, or sit with them at lunch.
challenges.why: First graders in Olpe showed up together for a classmate on adoption day. Saving a seat at lunch, or inviting someone into a game, tells a classmate they belong.
challenges.school: At recess, students invite one classmate who is playing alone to join a game that is already going.
challenges.home: Teach a sibling or cousin a game you like, and let them go first.
challenges.neighborhood: On an outing with a grown-up you live with, let another child in your own group take a turn first. Stay with your grown-up.
challenges.teacherNote: Watch the invitation so it stays welcome, and let a student say no. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is inviting a classmate into a game or to sit with you at lunch.

challenges.challenge: Make a paper ribbon and give it to a classmate who makes your class kinder.
challenges.why: At a pep rally in Mahanoy City, a student handed his homecoming crown to a friend. A paper ribbon for someone who makes the class kinder is a way to pass that kindness on.
challenges.school: Students make paper ribbons for classmates. The teacher helps the sharing stay kind, and every student can also make one to take home.
challenges.home: Make a paper ribbon for someone in your family and tell them one kind thing they do.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, tell a librarian, coach, or troop leader you already know one specific kind thing they do. Stay together.
challenges.teacherNote: Help the class notice kind acts, not popularity. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a paper ribbon for someone who makes your class kinder.

challenges.challenge: Spend ten quiet minutes caring for an animal you already live with, or draw a picture about animal care if you do not have a pet.
challenges.why: A shelter dog in Cincinnati went home after people helped with the things he needed. Ten quiet minutes with a pet you already know, or a drawing about animal care, practices that same attention.
challenges.school: Students draw an animal and write one sentence about what that animal needs. Leave pets at home.
challenges.home: With a grown-up, refill a water bowl, brush a pet, or tidy the spot where that pet rests. If you do not have a pet, draw one instead.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, borrow a library book about caring for animals. Do not approach an animal you do not know.
challenges.teacherNote: Pets stay home. The drawing is the classroom version. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is ten quiet minutes of care for a pet you already know, or a drawing if you do not have one.

challenges.challenge: With a grown-up at home, make a simple snack and share it with your family.
challenges.why: A bakery in Atlanta spends the year baking with adults who want a place to belong after high school. Making a snack at home and sharing it with your family is a free way to practice that welcome.
challenges.school: The class writes a no-cook snack idea to try at home. Do not ask students to bring food to share unless the school already allows it.
challenges.home: Make the snack with a grown-up and eat it together.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, drop a sealed snack you already have into a food drive your school is already running. Stay together.
challenges.teacherNote: Follow your school's food rules. Home is the place to make the snack. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is making a simple snack at home and sharing it with your family.

challenges.challenge: Draw a bright picture of your school or your street and put it where your family can see it.
challenges.why: Artists in Missoula finished the city's tallest mural in 22 days so people could look up and see it. A bright drawing on the fridge shares something cheerful with the people you live with.
challenges.school: Students draw the school and hang the pictures where the people who work there can see them.
challenges.home: Tape the drawing on the fridge or a bedroom door at home.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, notice one colorful thing on a walk and add it to the drawing when you get home. Stay together.
challenges.teacherNote: The drawings stay cheerful. Skip anything scary. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is a bright drawing of your school or street for the people you live with.

challenges.challenge: Spend twenty minutes helping at home by tidying a shared space, watering a plant, or sorting recycling.
challenges.why: About 150 volunteers in Arvada gave 450 hours to local groups, including a children's pantry. Twenty minutes of help at home is a free start, and it does not need a sign-up.
challenges.school: The class picks one shared job, such as wiping a table or putting books back, and does it together for twenty minutes.
challenges.home: Choose one job a grown-up lists, such as watering a plant or sorting recycling, and finish it.
challenges.neighborhood: With a grown-up you live with, pick up litter in your own yard or on your own block, using gloves that the grown-up provides. Stay together.
challenges.teacherNote: Pick a job every student can do, and stop at twenty minutes. Read the linked story aloud before the class starts. Do not send children off alone. Do not collect a child's name, age, school, or email.
challenges.shareText: This week's kindness challenge is twenty free minutes of help at home.
